messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 71
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Insurance Agent
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Stranger Interaction: Talking to strangers, Auditory (Sirens): Sirens, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Prevention: perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events
  Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
  Negative Appraisals: No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

The event itself was never spoken of, not then and not for decades after. What Harold remembered, when the fragments came, was not a single story with a beginning and an end, but pieces: the smell of whiskey on breath, the sound of a belt buckle hitting the floor, the particular screech of a siren passing outside the window of the small house where he grew up. He was seven, then eight, then nine. The man who was supposed to care for him was the one who delivered the blows, and afterward there was never an apology, never an acknowledgment, never a single consequence. Harold grew up, left that house, built a life. He became an insurance agent, a profession that required him to talk to strangers every day, to sit across from them at a desk and ask personal questions about their homes and their health and their loved ones. He learned to do it by keeping his mind occupied with the next question, the next form, the next policy detail. He never let himself pause. If he paused, the pieces could come.

Now, at seventy-one, Harold lives alone in a one-bedroom apartment. He is single, and has been for most of his adult life, though he would not say the two things are connected. He has come to believe that his body has a mind of its own, a traitorous organ that reacts as if the danger is still present even when he is standing in his own kitchen making coffee. A siren from the street outside will send his heart into his throat before his conscious mind has even registered the sound. The smell of alcohol on a passerby—a scent that reaches him in the grocery store aisle or on the sidewalk—will stop him cold, his palms damp, his vision narrowing, a taste like old pennies in his mouth. He knows, intellectually, that nothing is wrong. But his body does not seem to know. He has come to interpret this as a kind of betrayal written into his own flesh: the people who hurt him faced nothing, but his body still acts as though it is being hunted.

To manage this, Harold has developed a set of practices that he does not discuss with anyone. When he gets home from work, he stands at his front door and counts silently to seven before turning the lock. If he does not count, he is certain something bad will happen—though he cannot name what. He keeps the television on talk shows and news programs, never dramas or films about families or childhood. He will not watch anything that might resemble his own history, and he will not read books about it either. His mind must be occupied at all times. If he lets it go quiet, the fragments surface: not a full memory, but a flash of a wall, the smell of whiskey, the sound of a belt buckle, and then it is gone, leaving him shaken and confused. These fragments feel more real than the ordinary memories of his day. He can remember what he had for breakfast only vaguely, but the smell from forty years ago is as sharp as if the bottle were uncorked in the room.

At night, he listens. He lies in bed and tracks the sounds of the building: footsteps in the hallway, a door closing, the hum of the elevator. He tells himself this is vigilance, that it is reasonable for a man his age living alone. But he knows, somewhere beneath that rationalization, that he is listening for something else—someone entering. He has never been burgled. He has no reason to fear. And yet he reacts as if every creak is a threat. He has startled clients at his desk when they knocked on his office door, his body jerking before his mind could catch up, and he has had to laugh it off as being lost in thought. The false alarms exhaust him.

What finally brought Harold to seek help was a small thing, or seemed so. A new client came in last month, a man in his forties, and as he sat down Harold caught a faint smell of alcohol on his jacket. The man was perfectly pleasant, sober, there to update his life insurance. Harold excused himself to the restroom and stood over the sink for ten minutes, his hands gripping the porcelain, until the feeling passed. He realized then that he could not keep doing this. He is afraid of what his body will do next, and he is afraid of what he will lose if he cannot stop it. He does not expect to feel safe. He only wants to stop counting.
